subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Battery Storage Revolution
description: A quick win: understand The Battery Storage Revolution.

hook.text: In 2017, Elon Musk bet he could build the world's biggest battery in 100 days or it was free.

buildup.text: He won the bet. South Australia's battery saved millions in its first year of operation.

discovery.text: Lithium-ion battery costs dropped 97% since 1991, making grid storage suddenly affordable.

twist.text: New chemistries like iron-air and sodium-ion promise even cheaper long-duration storage.

climax.text: Grid batteries can respond in milliseconds — faster than any power plant can ramp up.

punchline.text: The grid's best backup fits in a shipping container.

quiz.question: How much have lithium-ion battery costs dropped since 1991?

details.summary: Battery energy storage systems allow excess renewable electricity to be stored and dispatched when the sun is not shining or wind is not blowing. Lithium-ion costs have fallen over 90 percent since 2010, and grid-scale battery installations are growing exponentially worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Storage solves renewables' intermittency problem. Affordable batteries make it possible to run grids on high shares of solar and wind without sacrificing reliability.
takeaways: Lithium-ion battery costs have dropped over 90 percent since 2010
Grid-scale batteries can respond to demand in milliseconds
Storage enables higher renewable penetration on power grids

faq.question: How long can grid batteries store energy?
faq.answer: Most lithium-ion grid batteries provide two to four hours of storage. Longer durations of eight hours or more are possible but costlier. For seasonal storage lasting weeks to months, alternative technologies like hydrogen or compressed air are needed.

faq.question: What materials are used in grid batteries?
faq.answer: Lithium-ion dominates, using lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Lithium iron phosphate cells avoid cobalt and are gaining share. Emerging alternatives include sodium-ion, iron-air, and flow batteries that use abundant, cheaper materials.
